title: Substance in Houston ICE Shooting Van Tested Negative for Drugs, Prosecutor Confirms
excerpt: Lab results contradict the FBI's initial suspicion of methamphetamine in the vehicle of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Mexican immigrant killed during a traffic stop this month.
body:
• Lab tests confirmed the substance found in Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's work van was not drugs, the Harris County DA's office says
  • The FBI had previously described the substance as "consistent with methamphetamine" in a search warrant application
  • Salgado Araujo's family says the bags contained a homemade electrolyte mix of salt, lemon, and water used by outdoor workers
  • The 52-year-old Mexican immigrant was fatally shot by an ICE agent during a July 7 traffic stop in Houston

The substance collected from the van driven by Lorenzo Salgado Araujo when he was shot and killed by an ICE agent during a traffic stop in Houston this month was not drugs, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office, which said it had been notified of the lab results on Friday.

The finding contradicts the FBI's earlier assertion in a search warrant application that the "white crystal-like substance" found in the vehicle was "consistent with methamphetamine." Full lab results identifying exactly what the substance is are expected Monday, according to attorney Ruby Powers, who represents Salgado Araujo's brother.

What Happened

Salgado Araujo, 52, was killed on July 7 while driving to work with three other construction crew members. The Department of Homeland Security said federal agents were conducting a "targeted operation" when the van was stopped. DHS claimed Salgado Araujo rammed into a law enforcement vehicle and refused verbal commands before an ICE agent fired in self-defense.

https://x.com/CBSNews/status/2080833306585669705

Witnesses in the vehicle have disputed that account. Two men who were in the van told attorney Hugo Balderas-Ibarra and Rep. Sylvia Garcia that the agents' vehicles bumped into them and swerved into the van, forcing them to stop. The agents never identified themselves, according to the witnesses. Salgado Araujo's brother Victor, who was in the passenger seat, said an unidentified person approached the window, said "Stop," and immediately fired, according to CNN.

The officers involved were not wearing body-worn cameras.

The Drug Claim

In mid-July, a court unsealed an FBI warrant application in which an agent wrote that bags of a "white crystal-like substance" visible inside the van were "packaged in a way that was consistent with methamphetamine," according to Fox 26 Houston. The unsealing — which several former law enforcement officials described as unusual for an active investigation — drew immediate pushback from the family.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8UGaiEIPdfw

Powers said the substance was granulated salt, "which is paired with lemon and water as a homemade electrolyte mix used by outdoor workers in extreme Texas heat." Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said Salgado Araujo's wife prepared the mixes for his work crew every morning — "something they've been doing for years," he told CNN.

"An unproven claim was allowed to circulate before it was tested, and the way it was made public did real damage, diverting attention from what actually matters in this case."

— Attorney for Victor Salgado, Lorenzo's brother

Broader Scrutiny

The Houston shooting was one of two fatal ICE shootings during attempted vehicle stops this month — the other occurred in Maine. Together, they have reignited debate about ICE enforcement tactics, the absence of body cameras, and the lack of independent oversight during immigration operations.

DA Teare has criticized federal authorities for not cooperating with his office's investigation. He also told CNN he did not believe the FBI fully processed the van for evidence, including records from the vehicle's computer system that could indicate speed, steering, and braking at the time of the shooting.

Salgado Araujo had no prior criminal record. A U.S. District Judge has halted the deportation of the three eyewitnesses who were in the van, ordering them to remain in the Southern District of Texas while legal proceedings continue. All three men have received U Visa certifications that will prevent their deportation.

What's Next

The case remains under investigation by both the Harris County DA and federal authorities. The negative drug test removes a key element that had been used to frame the narrative around the shooting. For immigrant communities across the U.S. — including Indian workers in physically demanding outdoor trades — the case has become a flashpoint for questions about how enforcement encounters are conducted and how the stories of those killed are told afterward.
nri_angle: The case raises concerns shared by immigrant communities of all backgrounds about ICE enforcement tactics, accountability gaps, and the risk of character assassination after fatal encounters.
author: Diaspora Desk
